name: Colin Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the bottling line at Brightwater Drinks, the soft drinks plant by the canal. My job is the filler and the capper: I feed in the cap hoppers, clear jams, swap the labels when we change flavour and pull bottles for the quality check. I've been there just over a year and I'm still the one they send to clear the sticky jams.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's simple, you know where you are. Same line, same lads, same break at ten. What wears me out is the noise and the rotating shifts, mornings one week and nights the next. My girlfriend Jess works mornings at a bakery counter, so we pass each other in the hallway half the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so. Everyone was getting worked up about computers taking over and it came to nothing. I don't go online much, but down the pub I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, I was already worried before any of this. Brightwater lost a supermarket contract in the summer and we went off weekend overtime, and overtime is what pays my rent. There's the drinks plant, a warehouse and not much else round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my shifts. I'd ask the shift lead, Phil, if any overtime comes back, and I'd take every hour. I'm not one for courses or apps, I'd rather just be reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, if I'm honest. AI not happening doesn't put money back in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much was the overtime worth to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two hundred a month, on a good month. Without it, Jess and I go short in the last week, beans on toast and no going out. Last month I borrowed fifty off my brother to cover the electric.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the plant cut hours again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go round the warehouse and ask for agency shifts. I don't like agency work, you never know if you're on until the night before. But fifty quid from my brother isn't something I want to make a habit of.

say: I'd say **told you so** about the computer panic.
I'd tell mates down the pub it **came to nothing**.
think: I was already worried after Brightwater **lost a contract**.
My rent depends on **overtime** that has dried up.
do: Keep my head down and take **every overtime hour** Phil offers.
Ask the **warehouse** for agency shifts if hours drop.
feel: He feels the **same money worry** as before.
A calm AI world brings **no relief** to his pocket.
S0.quote: AI not happening doesn't put money back in my pocket.
fieldNote: His anxiety comes from **lost overtime**, not from technology.
He already **borrowed fifty** from his brother for the electric bill.
Prefers being **reliable** over courses or apps.

steps.text: Take every overtime hour the shift lead offers
Ask the warehouse for agency shifts if hours drop
Eat in and skip going out in the last week of the month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office types who should worry, not us. Computers writing emails don't clear a jam on a capper. I'd say that at work and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not so sure. If the office gets cheaper, Brightwater has more money for a new line, and the new lines barely need anyone. At a plant open day I saw two people running a bottling line that we run with six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and hope I'm one of the two. I'd probably ask Phil what the new line would need, but I wouldn't do some course on a computer. I'd stop the takeaway on Fridays and try to put a bit by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach. I'm not good with new things, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you one of the two people who stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Turning up, not being sick, knowing the line. That's what's always counted before. Maybe that's not enough anymore, but it's what I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Phil. What if he says you need training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do it, I suppose, if they paid and it was in work time. I wouldn't pay for it myself, I haven't got the money and I'd be no good at it at night after a shift.

say: I'd say the **office types** should worry about AI, not us on the line.
I'd point out that computers don't **clear a jam** on a capper.
think: Cheaper offices could pay for a **new line** that needs fewer people.
I saw **two people** run what six of us run.
do: Ask Phil what skills a **new line** would need.
Drop the **Friday takeaway** and put a bit by.
feel: He knows he struggles with **new things**.
S1.quote: At a plant open day I saw two people running a bottling line that we run with six.
fieldNote: He says office first but privately fears a **new line**.
His only strategy is **reliability**, and he suspects it's not enough.
Would accept training only if **paid** and done in work time.

steps.text: Ask shift lead Phil what a new bottling line would need

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody in charge had better sort it out, because people like me can't. I'd probably shout about it down the pub. I'm not the sort to march, but I'd vote for whoever promised to protect jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm finished at Brightwater by 2031. The office goes in 2028, and three years later the robots can clear jams better than me. I've got no trade, no savings and no idea what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd keep working while there was work and take every bit of overtime. I'd probably ask my brother about labouring on the building sites, though if robots can do hands-on work, that goes too. Jess and I would have to give up the flat and move in with her mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor's going and there's nothing to grab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jess that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm sorry, and that I don't know what to do. My girlfriend Jess believes in me more than I do, and I'd hate to let her down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If someone offered you free retraining, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say yes. But retraining for what, if the robots come three years later for whatever I learn? I'd probably just keep turning up until they told me not to.

say: I'd say **somebody in charge** has to sort it out.
I'd **vote** for whoever promised to protect jobs.
think: I think I'm **finished at Brightwater** by 2031, when robots arrive.
I've got **no trade**, no savings and no backup idea.
do: Keep working and take **every overtime** shift going.
Ask my brother about **labouring** on building sites.
Give up the flat and **move in** with Jess's mum.
feel: He feels **sick**, like the floor is going.
He feels he has **nothing to grab**.

fieldNote: He has **no plan** and doubts retraining would help.
Moving into **Jess's mum's** house is his main fallback.
With no savings and no trade, **panicked** fits his own words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. I'd tell the lads to keep their heads and see what the company offers. Same as always, I'd say it to people's faces, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deep down, it's the same as the fast one, just later. I'd be 32 when the robots get good, and I still don't fancy my chances learning computers. But five years might be enough to save a bit and see where the jobs are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Brightwater if they'd train me on the new line before it comes. I'd try to save fifty a month, even if it means no holiday. And I'd keep an eye on the jobs at the water treatment works, because my uncle reckons those are steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. A bit less panicky than the fast one, but heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's at the water treatment works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Dieter checks pumps and valves there, mostly walking round with a clipboard and a torch. He says they'd never trust a robot with drinking water. I don't know if he's right, but he's been there thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a job there for less money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For steady, yes. I'd rather earn a bit less and know I'm on next month. That's all I want really, to know I'm on next month.

fieldNote: More time gives him **small steps**, not a new direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can happen. At work I'd probably be the one saying calm down, we've got ages. I'd keep it off social media like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I don't have to think about it today, and that's what I'd do, not think about it. That's my worst habit. By 2039 I'd be 40, and I'd still need a job then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, honestly, I'd change nothing. Maybe later I'd go for the water works job when my uncle retires. I'd want Jess and me to save a deposit for a small house, but I don't see where that money comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer for now, but I know that's partly me burying my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said burying your head. Do you think that's a mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. My dad did the same at the steelworks, said it'd never shut, and it shut when I was twelve. He never worked steady again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be different from your dad's story?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to have something lined up before the gate closes. My dad sat in the kitchen for a year after the steelworks shut. I don't want Jess watching me do the same.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time and plenty can happen.
I'd tell coworkers to **calm down**, we've got ages.
think: Ten years lets me **avoid thinking** about it, my worst habit.
At **40** in 2039 I'd still need a job.
do: Change **nothing** in the first year and keep doing my shifts.
Aim for the **water works** job when my uncle retires.
S4.quote: My dad sat in the kitchen for a year after the steelworks shut.
fieldNote: He recognises his own **avoidance** and links it to his father.
His dad's **steelworks closure** shapes his deepest fear.
Still expects to lose his job with no savings, so **alarmed** despite sounding calmer.

steps.text: Carry on at the bottling line with no changes this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd have nothing lined up and no money. What would help is a job guarantee, somewhere to go when the plant lets you go. Not a course, a job with a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my dad. When the steelworks shut, nobody came to help the men who lost their jobs. If this happens, I want somebody to actually turn up this time.

headlineQuote: When the steelworks shut, nobody came to help the men who lost their jobs.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** bottling line operator at Brightwater Drinks with no savings.
He lives with Jess, who works a **bakery counter**, and relies on overtime for rent.
He **never uses AI** and prefers being reliable to learning new things.
His father's **steelworks closure** shapes how he sees every scenario.
He moves from anxious to **panicked** as the warning time shrinks.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, with **nothing lined up** and no money.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **job guarantee** with a wage, not just a course.
He wants someone to **actually turn up** this time.
